Mersenne Primes. A Mersenne prime is a prime number of the form two to the power of p minus one, where p is itself prime. Named after the French monk Marin Mersenne, these numbers have fascinated mathematicians for centuries and include some of the largest known primes, discovered through intensive computational searches. Mersenne primes have the form M sub p equals two to the power of p minus one, where p is prime. If M sub p is prime, it is a Mersenne prime. Note that not all such numbers are prime. Examples include M sub two equals three, M sub three equals seven, M sub five equals thirty-one, and M sub seven equals one hundred twenty-seven. The first non-prime Mersenne number is M sub eleven, which equals two thousand forty-seven, equal to twenty-three times eighty-nine. As of recent counts, only around fifty Mersenne primes are known despite intensive searching. The gaps between consecutive discoveries can span years or even decades. The Great Internet Mersenne Prime Search, known as GIMPS, is a distributed computing project dedicated to finding new Mersenne primes. Every known perfect number, a number equal to the sum of its proper divisors, is even and related to Mersenne primes through the Euclid-Euler theorem. For instance, six equals one plus two plus three, and twenty-eight equals one plus two plus four plus seven plus fourteen. The connection between perfect numbers and Mersenne primes remains one of the deepest mysteries in number theory. This relationship links Mersenne primes to Marin Mersenne, the mathematician who investigated them and gave them his name. Understanding which Mersenne numbers are composite informs the search and connects to prime factorization. The existence of infinitely many Mersenne primes remains unknown, an open question that parallels other deep conjectures about the infinite nature of special prime forms.
